Since at the moment we do not know if the length of that message is important (see Section 1.4 on open questions), we do not include details on this modification. 1.2.2 Trusted measurement provers Given an amplified XZ Hamiltonian H = 12 (ΠZ + ΠX ) on Bq qubits provided as input, we warm up by describing a simple verification protocol in the case of a “trusted measurement prover.” This is a fictional prover (considered only for the purpose of this introduction) who holds an arbitrary quantum state |φ⟩W of M qubits and returns M -bit measurement outcomes of |φ⟩W in the computational (Z) or Hadamard (X) basis whenever asked to do so. Then the following simple, classical protocol would work. Since the verifier is only allowed to access a small number of bits of any outcome reported by the prover, and we do not assume any promise on the degree or locality of H (so a small number of bit or phase flips can potentially affect the energy by a lot), it is sensible to require |φ⟩W to be an encoding of a ground state |Γ⟩ of H using a suitable quantum error correcting code. Thus let Cq (q for “quantum”) be an [M, Bq , dq ] quantum error correcting code with linear distance dq ∝ M , such that Cq is furthermore a CSS code with parity check matrices (HX , HZ ). Let Eq the unitary encoding map of Cq , and |φ⟩W = Eq (|Γ⟩W |0⟩S ) where |0⟩S are ancilla qubits required for the encoding process. Now suppose the verifier chooses a basis W ∈ {X, Z} at random and requests measurement outcomes obtained from measuring |φ⟩W in the basis W . The trusted measurement prover obliges, sending outcomes w ∈ {0, 1}M . The verifier then samples a projection ΠW j in such a way that ΠW = Ej ΠW j . Since it is diagonal in basis W , the constraint ΠW j can be represented by a boolean function fj : {0, 1}Bq → {0, 1} (we suppress the dependence on † ⊗Bq W for clarity) such that ΠW P j = x fj (x)SW |x⟩⟨x| SW , where SW = I if W = Z and ⊗Bq SW = H if W = X. Furthermore, we can represent the function fj as a “logical” function fj′ : {0, 1}M → {0, 1} by using logical operators for the code Cq .7 For reasons that will soon become clear, define fej = fj′ ◦ EW ◦ DW , where EW and DW are the encoding and decoding maps associated with the linear code CW = ker HW respectively.8 The goal of the verifier is to check that fj′ (w) = 0. If w ∈ CW , as it would be in case |φ⟩W is the intended witness, this is equivalent to checking that fej (w) = 0. So, it is enough for the verifier to check that w ∈ CW AND fej (w) = 0. Since it cannot do either task by itself (in particular, fej is nonlocal) it will enlist the prover’s help. To explain this first recall that a PCP of proximity (PCPP) for an (efficiently computable) statement of the form “g(y) = 0” is a proof π that guarantees that y is close to a string y ′ such that g(y ′ ) = 0, and such that verifying π only requires reading a constant number of bits of y and π. 7 Somewhat informally, we map a string x ∈ {0, 1}M to x′ ∈ {0, 1}Bq by evaluating the logical operators, i.e. x′ = Kx where the rows of K represent the support of logical operators for Cq in basis W . We refer to the definition of fe from f in Section 3 for the precise methodology. 8 Note that CW does not necessarily have distance. The only property we will need is that the decoder DW decodes a small syndrome to an error whose size is not much bigger. This property is satisfied by the decoder in basis W for the code we use, see Section 1.2.5 and Section 2.4.
